title: 152 Movement patterns of beef bulls during the breeding season in Southcentral Montana
content:
Abstract
The performance of bulls is critical to the success of rangeland livestock producers, however, there is little information quantifying their behavioral ecology during the breeding season. This study evaluated the influence of age on the movement patterns of beef bulls across the breeding season. Thirty-six commercial, Angus-based bulls were equipped with electronic global positioning system (GPS) ear tags and monitored for the first six weeks of the breeding season. On July 16th, 2024, the bulls were turned out into 5 rangeland pastures in southcentral Montana, varying in size between 968 and 7,833 ha. Bulls were categorized into three ages classes: young (1-2 years old), mature (3-4 years old), and old (5-8 years old). GPS tags recorded fixes every five minutes. Distance traveled and turning angle were calculated between successive fixes. Daily, weekly, and season-long range sizes were determined using 95% kernel density isopleths. Data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models. Mean daily distance traveled decreased from 9.4 km in week one to 5.3 km in week six (P < 0.01). Young bulls exhibited a linear decrease, while mature and old bulls exhibited quadratic decreases (P < 0.01). In four of the six weeks, we detected no differences in distance traveled between age classes (P ≥ 0.18). We detected no differences in mean turning angle between age classes (P = 0.35), however, all bulls exhibited a linear decrease in mean turning angle over the breeding season. Range size varied by age class, and temporal window (P < 0.01). Young bulls had the largest mean daily range size (165 ha; P ≤ 0.01), old bulls had the smallest (98 ha; P < 0.01), and mature bulls intermediate (138 ha; P ≤ 0.01). Young bulls also had a larger season-long range size than mature and old bulls (1282 vs. 494 ha, respectively; P < 0.01). Weekly range size varied by age class, where young bulls varied across the season (P < 0.01), mature bulls had no trend (P ≥ 0.47), and old bulls a tendency for a linear decrease (P = 0.08). These results catalogue changes in bull movement patterns during the breeding season. All bulls decreased distance traveled and mean turning angle over the course of the breeding season, which can indicate a decrease in searching behavior. This would be consistent with successively fewer cows in heat. Bulls from all age classes largely traveled the same amount over the breeding season, however, younger bulls occupied larger areas than older bulls and were less consistent about the areas they were occupying. This may be due to differences in socio-spatial hierarchies or experience.
